examples.professional: The sequencing pipeline flagged an unusual duplication on chromosome 7 in the tumor sample.
examples.analytical: Mendel's inheritance patterns became fully explicable only after scientists located genes along the chromosome.

nuance.analogy: A chromosome is like a bookshelf, and each gene is one book shelved on it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek chrōma (color) and sōma (body), because the structure takes up dye readily under a microscope.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'kro-MO-some'. The stress belongs on the first syllable.
Pronouncing the ch as 'sh', as in 'SHROH-muh-sohm'. It is a k sound.

chromosome.etymology: 19th century: from German *Chromosom*, ultimately from Ancient Greek *χρῶμα* (“colour”) + *σῶμα* (“body”).

senses.definition: In AI: Splitting long documents into smaller pieces so they can be embedded and retrieved.

A method of presenting information which splits concepts into small pieces or "chunks" of information to make reading and understanding faster and easier, using such methods as bulleted lists, short subheadings, or short sentences with one or two ideas per sentence.
The division of memory or data etc. into smaller units for easier processing.
The process of reducing something to short, thick pieces, usually using a hammer or a crowbar.
A strategy for making more efficient use of short-term memory by recoding information.
The partial-quotients method for solving simple division problems by repeated subtraction.

core.definition: In AI, splitting long documents into smaller pieces so they can be embedded and retrieved by a search or language model.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, CHUNK. The n before k is not a separate sound; it merges into the ng sound, so say chunk as one syllable that rhymes with junk, not chun-king with a clear n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in AI and psychology, with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: In an AI or data team you will hear chunking in design reviews, as in our chunking strategy or fixed-size chunking. In psychology it refers to grouping information into units. Americans also say chunk or chunking casually to mean breaking work into pieces, such as let's chunk this project into two-week sprints.

distinctions.note: Tokenization splits text into model tokens, often words or subwords, while chunking groups text into larger passages meant for retrieval.
Segmentation is the general term for dividing text, images or audio; chunking specifically means passages sized for embedding and search.

examples.everyday: I'm chunking my study time into twenty-five-minute blocks so I don't burn out.
examples.professional: We need to test a few chunking strategies before we re-index the support documents.
examples.analytical: Chunking embeds a theory of meaning, since the boundaries we choose decide which ideas a retrieval system treats as one unit.

nuance.analogy: Like cutting a long loaf into slices so each one fits on a plate.
nuance.etymology: From chunk, a thick lump; the exact origin of chunk is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using chunking to mean a single piece; the process is chunking and one piece is a chunk.
Stressing the second syllable, saying chunk-ING instead of CHUNK-ing.

conversation.text: Chunking splits long documents into smaller passages before we embed them.
Our chunking cuts tables in half, which is why the numeric questions fail.
In psychology, chunking means grouping information into units so it's easier to remember.

senses.definition: To cover with a cladding or another material (for example, insulation).
To imbue (with a specified quality); to envelop or surround.
Wearing clothing or some other covering (for example, an armour) on the body; clothed, dressed.
Covered, enveloped in, or surrounded by a cladding, or a specified material or substance.
Adorned, ornamented.

core.definition: Wearing clothing or covered with a specified material, such as armor or a protective layer.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short 'a' vowel as in 'cat' and end with a clear 'd'. Many learners mistakenly lengthen the vowel to 'klayd'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly elevated. It sounds more descriptive or poetic than everyday dressing words.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use clad mainly in writing, news descriptions, literature and occasionally in formal speech. In casual conversation, people normally say 'dressed in' or 'wearing'. It is common in phrases like 'clad in black' or 'clad in armor'.

distinctions.note: Dressed is the everyday word for wearing clothes, while clad is more formal and descriptive.
Clothed is neutral and common, while clad is stylized and often used for dramatic or literary effect.

examples.everyday: She showed up at the party clad in a bright red jacket.
examples.professional: The new server racks are clad in aluminum panels to help disperse heat.
examples.analytical: The argument is clad in technical language, but its central claim is ethical and not merely empirical.

nuance.analogy: Clad is like a costume that the word itself wears: it dresses up a plain description.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English cladde, past participle of clathen, to clothe, from Old English clāthian.
common_mistakes: Using clad as a verb in everyday speech, when 'dressed' or 'wearing' is more natural.
Lengthening the vowel to 'klayd' instead of the short 'a' sound.

clad.etymology: From Middle English *clad*, *cladde*, *cled*, *cledde*, past tense and past participle forms of *clethen* (“ to put clothing on, clothe, dress; to provide clothing to; to arm, equip; to cover, envelop; to conceal; to adorn”), from Old English *clǣþan*…

senses.definition: The gentle or kind exercise of power; leniency, mercy; compassion in judging or punishing.
A pardon, commutation, or similar reduction, removal, or postponement of legal penalties by an executive officer of a state.
(rare) Mildness of weather.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Mercy shown by a judge or ruler, such as reducing a punishment or granting a pardon.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is weak, so the vowel is /ən/, and the final -cy sounds like 'see', not 'sigh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It presents mercy as a deliberate act by someone with legal power, and it sounds serious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use clemency mostly in legal and political news, as in 'the governor granted clemency to the inmate.' In everyday talk, people say 'mercy' or 'a break'. A clemency request is a formal petition, usually made by a lawyer to a governor or the president. Do not use it for ordinary forgiveness between friends.

distinctions.note: A pardon fully forgives a crime; clemency is the broader category that includes pardons, commutations, and reprieves.
Mercy is a general quality of compassion; clemency is an official act by someone with legal authority.
Leniency is a general softness in punishing and can be informal; clemency is formal and official.

examples.everyday: I'm not asking for clemency, Mom, I just want a second chance.
examples.professional: Legal asked the governor's office to review clemency for three inmates whose sentences were excessive.
examples.analytical: Clemency reveals a moral tension: power is exercised outside the rules, yet it can correct what the rules get wrong.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee waving off a penalty after the rules were technically broken.
nuance.etymology: From Latin clementia, mildness or gentleness, from clemens, mild or merciful.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'clemancy' by analogy with other -ancy nouns; the correct spelling is clemency.
Using it for ordinary personal forgiveness, which sounds too legal and stiff.

senses.definition: To become cloudy or overcast.
senses.example: The sky is clouding over. I hope you have an umbrella.

core.definition: To become covered with clouds, so the sky gradually loses its brightness and turns gray.

pronunciation.tip: The particle over gets the main stress in this phrasal verb, so cloud has only a weaker stress. Don't say 'KLOWD over' with equal stress, and keep the ow diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a change in weather, though it can also suggest a shift in mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say cloud over mainly about the sky in weather talk, such as 'It's clouding over' when the sun disappears. It is casual to standard and fits conversation with friends, coworkers, and neighbors. For a sudden change, Americans might say 'the sky clouded up' in some regions.

distinctions.note: Cloud over describes the change as it happens, while overcast describes a sky that is already fully covered.
Cloud up is more often used for windows, glasses, or mirrors that fog, while cloud over is the usual phrase for the sky.

examples.everyday: Let's hike early before the sky clouds over.
examples.professional: The forecast says it'll cloud over by noon, so the outdoor photo shoot may need to move.
examples.analytical: The sky clouds over gradually, and the change in light marks a shift from clarity to uncertainty.

nuance.analogy: Clouding over is like a curtain slowly being drawn across a window.
nuance.etymology: Cloud comes from Old English clūd meaning rock or hill, later applied to masses of vapor; over comes from Old English ofer.
common_mistakes: Confusing cloud over, the change, with cloudy, the state; say 'It's clouding over' for a change happening now and 'It's cloudy' for the current condition.
Assuming cloud over means rain; it refers only to cloud cover.

conversation.text: It clouded over right when we got to the beach.
The sky clouded over, so we packed up early.
It usually clouds over in the afternoon up in the mountains.

senses.definition: The edge of the land where it meets an ocean, sea, gulf, bay, or large lake.
senses.example: The rocky coast of Maine has few beaches.

senses.definition: To glide along without adding energy; to allow a vehicle to continue moving forward after disengaging the engine or ceasing to apply motive power.
senses.example: When I ran out of gas, fortunately I managed to coast into a nearby gas station.

senses.definition: To make a minimal effort; to continue to do something in a routine way, without initiative or effort.
To sail along a coast.

core.definition: The land along the edge of an ocean, sea, or large lake, where the land meets the water.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long 'oh' glide, so avoid the short 'o' of 'cost'. In the verb sense, stress is the same, but the meaning shifts to moving without effort.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. In travel or real estate contexts it can sound appealing, as in living near the coast.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the coast' when they mean the region along the ocean, often with a name such as 'the West Coast' or 'the East Coast'. People say 'on the coast' or 'at the coast' for a location, and 'up the coast' or 'down the coast' for directions along it. The verb 'to coast' is common informally too, as in 'I'm just coasting at work,' meaning doing the minimum.

distinctions.note: Shore is the land right at the water's edge, while coast refers to a wider region along the sea.
Coast is the land area itself, while coastline is the outline or boundary where land meets sea.

examples.everyday: We're spending the weekend up the coast in Maine.
examples.professional: Our regional sales team covers the entire East Coast.
examples.analytical: Coastal erosion is most visible where the coast meets the storm surge of open water.

nuance.analogy: The coast is like a hinge between land and sea, the place where one world hands off to the other.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'coste', meaning side or rib, from Latin 'costa', meaning rib or side.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'coast' with 'cost', which has a different vowel.
Using 'coast' for a location far inland, since it only refers to the seashore region.

coast.etymology: From Middle English *coste* (“rib; side of the body”), from Old French *coste* (“rib; side of an object; coast”), from Latin *costa* (“rib; side, wall”).

conversation.text: We're driving down the coast next week and stopping in a few small towns.
She grew up on the East Coast, so she's used to cold winters.
It's always a few degrees cooler on the coast than inland.

senses.definition: Given to fighting; disposed to engage in combat; pugnacious.
senses.example: Their combative conduct leads to many problems.

core.definition: Eager to argue, fight or oppose others; ready to engage in conflict.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the vowel is a short a as in 'cat'. The final -ive is a reduced vowel, so say 'tiv', not 'teeve'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most workplace and social contexts, since it suggests hostility. It is neutral when describing athletes or competitors.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use combative for people who enjoy arguing or who seem ready to fight. It sounds more formal than 'argumentative' or 'pushy'. It describes a personality or stance, as in 'he gets combative in meetings'. In sports or combat sports it is neutral.

distinctions.note: Argumentative focuses on liking to argue; combative suggests a more aggressive, hostile readiness to fight.
Pugnacious is more literary and stresses a tendency to pick fights; combative is more common in everyday and professional speech.

examples.everyday: My uncle gets really combative whenever politics comes up at dinner.
examples.professional: Our product manager sounded combative in the review, so the rest of the team stopped offering ideas.
examples.analytical: Hobbes portrays humans in a state of nature as combative, driven by competition, diffidence and glory.

nuance.analogy: Like a boxer who keeps stepping into the ring even when the bell hasn't rung.
nuance.etymology: From French combatif, from combattre 'to fight', from Latin combattere.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KUM-buh-tiv) instead of the second.
Confusing combative with combatant; a combatant is a person in a fight, while combative describes a temperament.

senses.definition: Very interesting; able to capture and hold one's attention.
senses.example: The novel was so compelling that I couldn't put it down.

senses.definition: Capable of causing someone to believe or agree.
senses.example: He made a compelling argument.

senses.definition: Strong and forceful; that causes one to feel like they must do something; necessitating action.
senses.example: I would need a very compelling reason to leave my job.

senses.definition: An act of compulsion; an obliging somebody to do something.

core.definition: So interesting, convincing or forceful that it holds your attention or makes you want to act.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PEL, with a short e as in 'pet'. The -ing ending is a short 'ing' sound, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most uses: a compelling story, argument or offer. It can be neutral when describing an obligation, as in 'a compelling reason to leave', and it is strong praise in reviews and marketing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use compelling constantly in reviews, pitches, news and everyday talk: 'That's a compelling argument' or 'a compelling reason to switch'. It sounds more thoughtful than 'cool' and more lively than 'good'. A 'compelling offer' in a store means a deal that is hard to turn down.

distinctions.note: Convincing focuses on making you believe something; compelling also means it grips your attention and may push you to act.
Interesting is a mild everyday word; compelling is stronger and implies that the thing demands your attention.
Persuasive describes an argument that wins people over; compelling can describe a story, image or situation as well as an argument.

examples.everyday: That new series sounds compelling, so let's watch the first episode tonight.
examples.professional: The A/B test shows compelling evidence that the shorter checkout flow increases conversions.
examples.analytical: Hume's critique of induction is compelling because it shows that past regularities alone cannot justify expecting the same future.

nuance.analogy: A compelling idea is like a song that gets stuck in your head: it holds you until you act on it.
nuance.etymology: From the present participle of Latin compellere 'to drive together', from com- and pellere 'to drive'.
common_mistakes: Confusing compelling with compulsive; compulsive describes a person's behavior, while compelling describes something that attracts or convinces.
Using compelling to mean forced or required; it implies strong attraction or persuasion, not coercion.

senses.definition: To plan together; to settle or adjust by conference, agreement, or consultation.
To plan; to devise; to arrange.
To act in harmony or conjunction; to form combined plans.
An agreement in a design or plan; a union formed by mutual communication of opinions and views; an accordance in a scheme; harmony; a simultaneous action.
Musical accordance or harmony; concord.
A musical performance, usually public, in which several performers or instruments take part.
senses.example: I’m going to the rock concert on Friday.

core.definition: A live musical performance, usually public, where musicians or singers perform for an audience.

pronunciation.tip: In the noun sense for music, stress falls on the first syllable, KAHN. The verb meaning to plan together is different, stressed as kun-SURT, so don't use the verb's stress for the noun.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a lively, enjoyable event and is almost always used favorably.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say go to a concert for live music of any kind, from classical orchestras to rock and pop shows. For a small club performance, people more often say gig, show, or set, which sound more casual. In phrases like in concert with, the word can also mean working together, but in everyday use, concert refers to music.

distinctions.note: A recital is usually a performance by one or a few musicians, often classical, while a concert can feature a band, an orchestra, or multiple acts.
A gig is an informal term for a performance, often a small or club show, while concert sounds more formal and suggests a larger event.

examples.everyday: Do you want to grab tickets for the Saturday concert at the amphitheater?
examples.professional: We're sponsoring the summer concert series, so I need the venue contract signed by Friday.
examples.analytical: A concert depends on shared attention, since the meaning of the music emerges only when an audience listens together.

nuance.analogy: Like a potluck of sound, where each performer brings a dish, and the evening is the meal everyone shares.
nuance.etymology: From French concert, from Italian concerto, from Latin concertare 'to contend or strive together'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the noun on the second syllable, as in kun-SURT, which sounds like the verb
Using concert to mean any show, when a play, comedy act, or sports event would be called something else

conversation.text: We got tickets to a concert in the park.
The concert was amazing, but I can barely hear now.
Are you going to the concert on Saturday?

senses.definition: To forgive, excuse or overlook (something that is considered morally wrong, offensive, or generally disliked).
To allow, accept or permit (something that is considered morally wrong, offensive, or generally disliked).
To forgive (marital infidelity or other marital offense).

core.definition: To accept or overlook behavior you consider wrong, so that it goes unpunished or unchallenged.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, DOHN, which is a long vowel and a clear n. Learners often stress the first syllable, saying KON-dohn, which sounds like a different word.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most uses. Saying someone condones a behavior implies disapproval of the people who allowed it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in news, workplace policy, ethics discussions, and serious conversations, not for minor annoyances. It is often used in negative sentences, such as 'I don't condone' or 'We won't condone.' In casual talk, people say 'let it slide' or 'put up with it' instead.

distinctions.note: Tolerate means putting up with something; condone implies moral responsibility for allowing a wrong act, which makes it stronger.
Excuse focuses on reducing blame for a person; condone focuses on accepting the wrong act itself.
Forgive is a personal decision to let go of resentment toward someone; condone is about allowing the behavior, and it can be public.

examples.everyday: I'm not going to condone him yelling at the waiter, even if he had a bad day.
examples.professional: Our code of conduct does not condone harassment, and managers who ignore complaints will face discipline.
examples.analytical: A silent bystander may not endorse the act, but silence can still condone it in the eyes of the community.

nuance.analogy: Like a teacher who sees cheating and says nothing, letting it stand as acceptable.
nuance.etymology: From Latin condonare 'to give up, pardon', from con- 'altogether' and donare 'to give'.
common_mistakes: Confusing condone with condemn; condone means accept or overlook, while condemn means strongly criticize.
Using 'condone of' or 'condone for'; use it directly, as in 'condone violence'.
Stressing the first syllable as KON-dohn, which sounds like a different word.

senses.definition: The state or characteristic of being conscientious.

core.definition: The quality of being careful, thorough and dutiful about your work and responsibilities; a strong sense of duty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EN. The ti and ci spellings both sound like sh, and the last syllables are reduced to a quick uh sound. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names an admirable trait and is often used in personality research and job descriptions.
nuance.usage_note: In America, conscientiousness is common in psychology, human resources, and workplace talk, especially in the Big Five personality model. People might say someone has a lot of conscientiousness, but in everyday conversation they more often say she is really responsible or he is very careful. It can appear in hiring discussions and performance reviews.

distinctions.note: Diligence is persistent effort over time. Conscientiousness is a broader trait that includes care, reliability and a sense of duty.
Responsibility is the obligation itself or being accountable for something. Conscientiousness is the personal quality of meeting that obligation carefully.

examples.everyday: Her conscientiousness is why my dad trusts her to watch the house while we're away.
examples.professional: In the interview, the hiring manager asked how I demonstrate conscientiousness when deadlines change.
examples.analytical: Philosophers and psychologists alike have treated conscientiousness as a virtue that links personal character with social responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Think of a building inspector who checks every bolt: the trait is the steady habit of doing things right without being watched.
nuance.etymology: From conscientious, from Latin conscientia 'conscience,' from conscire 'to be conscious of.'
common_mistakes: Saying conscientiousity or adding an extra syllable at the end.
Using conscientiousness to mean being aware of something; for that, use consciousness or awareness.

senses.definition: Holy meditation.
The act of contemplating; being highly concentrated in thought; musing.
The act of looking forward to a future event.
The state of being considered or planned.
senses.example: contemplation of port facility expansion

core.definition: Deep, quiet thought; in Christian spirituality, silent, loving attention to God beyond words and discursive thought.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'PLAY', with a secondary stress on 'kahn'. The middle 'tum' is weak. Americans often skip the 'm' sound's separate syllable, so it sounds like 'kahn-tum-PLAY-shun'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and calm; it suggests depth and seriousness. It can be neutral when it means simply thinking about doing something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in everyday speech for serious thought ('lost in contemplation') and for 'considering' an action ('the contemplation of a move'). In Christian spirituality it names a form of prayer. It sounds more reflective and formal than 'thinking'.

distinctions.note: Meditation often involves actively reflecting on a text or idea; contemplation is a quieter, simpler resting in what is seen or loved.
Reflection is thinking back on something; contemplation is a sustained, focused gaze.
Consideration is weighing a matter to decide; contemplation does not need a decision.

examples.everyday: He sat on the porch in quiet contemplation, watching the sun go down.
examples.professional: After some contemplation, the team decided to rebuild the pipeline from scratch.
examples.analytical: For the desert fathers, contemplation was not an escape from the world but a purified way of seeing it and its Creator.

nuance.analogy: Contemplation is like looking at a mountain lake until the ripples settle and you see clearly to the bottom.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contemplatio, from contemplari, 'to observe, consider' (com- + templum, a space marked out for observation).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'contemplate' in pronunciation: the noun has stress on 'PLAY'.
Using it as a countable noun in the usual sense; it is mostly uncountable.
Saying 'contemplation about' instead of 'contemplation of'.
nuance.biblical_note: The word is not frequent in the RSV, but the idea appears. Psalm 27:4 speaks of beholding the beauty of the Lord, and Psalm 46:10 invites us to be still and know God. In 2 Corinthians 3:18 believers behold the glory of the Lord and are transformed. Greek theoria and Latin contemplatio became standard terms for this gaze in Christian tradition.

contemplation.etymology: From Middle English *contemplacioun*, from Old French *contemplation*, from Latin *contemplatio*.

senses.definition: A statement which is neither a tautology nor a contradiction.
The quality of being contingent, of happening by chance.
A possibility; something which may or may not happen. A chance occurrence, especially in finance, unexpected expenses.

An amount of money which a party to a contract has to pay to the other party (usually the supplier of a major project to the client) if they do not fulfill the contract according to the specification.

core.definition: A possible future event or circumstance that may or may not happen, often planned for as a backup.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TIN. The -gency ending is pronounced "jun-see," with the g sounding like a j. Avoid saying the g as a hard sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to something uncertain, and it is often used in planning contexts to mean being prepared.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contingency most often in business, project planning and emergency preparedness, as in contingency plan. In casual speech they would say backup plan or just in case. It sounds slightly formal, so it fits meetings and documents better than conversation.

distinctions.note: A possibility is any event that might happen. A contingency is specifically something that could happen and that you plan for.
An emergency is an event that has already happened and needs immediate action. A contingency is a future event you prepare for.

collocations: in the event of a contingency

examples.everyday: I packed an extra phone charger as a contingency in case the battery dies on the road trip.
examples.professional: We added a ten percent contingency to the budget in case the vendor delivers late.
examples.analytical: Hume argues that our belief in causal necessity rests on the contingency of experience, which never reveals a necessary connection.

nuance.analogy: A contingency plan is like a spare tire: you hope you never need it, but you keep it in the trunk anyway.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin contingentia, from contingere, to happen or touch on.
common_mistakes: Using contingency to mean emergency, as in "we had a big contingency yesterday" (say emergency).
Mispronouncing the g as a hard sound, as in kon-TIN-gen-see.

senses.definition: Which reverses the order of morphism composition: formally, which associates each morphism f:X→Y to a morphism F(f):F(Y)→F(X).
Scaling inversely with a change of basis.
Using or relating to contravariance.
A bihomogeneous polynomial in dual variables of x, y, and the coefficients of some homogeneous form in x, y, that is invariant under some group of linear transformations.

core.definition: Reversing the direction of a mapping, so that arrows or morphisms are inverted when composed, as in category theory.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on VAIR, the third syllable of the word, with a secondary stress on KAHN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contravariant almost exclusively in mathematics, especially category theory, algebraic geometry, and tensor analysis. It is precise and not used in everyday speech. Students often meet it alongside 'covariant,' so they should know both terms to describe how quantities transform in opposite ways.

distinctions.note: Covariant mappings preserve the direction of arrows; contravariant mappings reverse them.
Invariant means unchanged under a transformation; contravariant means the quantity changes, but in the opposite direction from the basis.

examples.everyday: My friend in grad school said the course on tensors was hard because of the contravariant terms.
examples.professional: The contravariant functor in our model reverses the direction of the mapping, which we need to account for in the code.
examples.analytical: A contravariant assignment sends each morphism to one in the opposite direction, a structure that organizes many dual constructions in algebraic geometry.

nuance.analogy: Like a mirror reversing the direction of a path that you walk along a line.
nuance.etymology: From contra-, against, plus variant, from Latin variare, to vary.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in KAHN-truh-vair-ee-unt.
Confusing it with contrary, which is a different word with a different meaning.

senses.definition: The group of test subjects left untreated or unexposed to some procedure and then compared with treated subjects in order to validate the results of the test.

core.definition: In an experiment, the group of subjects that does not receive the treatment, used as a baseline to compare with the treated group.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the second syllable of control, TROHL, while group is stressed on its single syllable. Keep the first syllable of control weak, so it sounds like 'kun' rather than 'KON.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It names a standard part of experimental design and carries no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use control group in science, medicine, psychology, business testing and data science. In casual talk you would not normally use it, but in a work meeting it is common when discussing A/B tests or clinical trials. Often people refer to it simply as 'the control' when the context is clear.

distinctions.note: The treatment group receives the intervention being tested, while the control group does not and provides the baseline for comparison.
A control variable is a factor kept constant across conditions, while a control group is a set of subjects who do not receive the treatment.

examples.everyday: My sister is part of a study where half the volunteers take the pill and the control group gets a sugar pill.
examples.professional: We compared the new checkout design against a control group that kept the old page, and conversion was only slightly higher.
examples.analytical: Without a control group, it is impossible to tell whether the drop in symptoms came from the treatment or from natural recovery.

nuance.analogy: A control group is like a plain sample in a cooking test: you need it to know whether the new ingredient really made a difference.
nuance.etymology: Control comes from Anglo-French contreroller, 'to keep a copy of accounts'; group comes from Italian gruppo, 'knot, cluster.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'control team' or 'control people' when the technical term is control group.
Pronouncing control with a strong first syllable, as in KON-trol, rather than kuhn-TROHL.

senses.definition: The quality of being a craftsman.
An example of a craftsman's work.
senses.example: The craftsmanship on the antique chair was exquisite.

core.definition: Skill and care shown in making something by hand, or an example of such skilled work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a reduced schwa. The final -ship has a short i, so say 'KRAFTS-mun-ship' with a clear sh ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises high quality, careful work, and attention to detail.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'craftsmanship' in product reviews, home improvement, design, and everyday praise, as in 'The craftsmanship on this table is amazing.' It can describe both the skill and the finished quality. A natural reply is 'Yes, they really take pride in their work.'

distinctions.note: Quality is a general word for how good something is; craftsmanship specifically highlights the skill and care of a maker.
Workmanship is close in meaning and more common in technical or business contexts, such as warranties; craftsmanship sounds more admiring and artistic.

examples.everyday: I love this old dresser; the craftsmanship is so much better than anything they sell at the furniture store now.
examples.professional: Our product team wants to emphasize craftsmanship in the new line of furniture to justify the higher price.
examples.analytical: The study argues that craftsmanship embodies a moral relationship between worker, material, and community that industrial production tends to erase.

nuance.analogy: Craftsmanship is like a signature written with care: each stroke shows the maker's attention and pride.
nuance.etymology: From craftsman plus -ship, a suffix denoting skill or state.
common_mistakes: Using craftsmanship for a single person; it refers to the skill or quality, so say 'a craftsman' for the person.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable with a full vowel, saying 'KRAFTS-man-ship' instead of the reduced 'mun'.

senses.definition: A rough, broken fragment of rock.
A game played with three dice, similar to Yahtzee.
A partially compacted bed of gravel mixed with shells, of the Pliocene to Pleistocene epochs.

core.definition: A steep, rough, broken rock or cliff projecting from a mountain or hillside.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a of 'cat' and a hard g, with the r clearly pronounced. The word is one syllable, so do not add a vowel before the final g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to vivid. It describes a rugged landscape and can suggest danger or strength.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'crag' mainly in hiking, climbing, nature writing, and literary description, as in 'We climbed up the crag above the lake.' In casual speech they might say 'cliff' or 'rock face' instead. The word often appears in descriptions of mountains, coastlines, and rugged terrain.

distinctions.note: A cliff is a broad steep face of rock, while a crag is usually a rougher, more jagged outcrop.
A boulder is a large rounded rock, not a steep projecting rock face or outcrop.

examples.everyday: We hiked up to the crag at the top of the trail, and the view of the valley was amazing.
examples.professional: The trail crew marked the loose rock on the crag so hikers would avoid the slippery edge.
examples.analytical: The poet uses the crag as an emblem of permanence, contrasting its fixed shape with the shifting weather of the valley below.

nuance.analogy: A crag is like a broken tooth of the mountain, jutting out sharply from the smoother slope.
nuance.etymology: Of Celtic origin, related to Welsh craig, rock.
common_mistakes: Using crag for any hill or mountain; it refers specifically to a rough rock outcrop.
Pronouncing the final g as a j or dropping it, which changes the word.
nuance.biblical_note: Crag appears in biblical poetry to describe rocky places of refuge and strength, often as a picture of God's protection. The Hebrew word behind many such images is 'tsur', meaning rock. Job 39:28 in the Revised Standard Version describes an eagle that dwells on the crag and makes its nest in a high, rocky place. Psalm 18:2 uses rock imagery to describe God as a fortress and refuge, and 1 Samuel 24:2 mentions the rocks of the wild goats, a rugged area where David hid from Saul.

crag.etymology: From 13th century Middle English *crag*, from *crec*, a contracted form of *carrac*, possibly ultimately from the late Proto-Indo-European/ **kar* (“stone, hard”); see also.

senses.definition: To pick or take someone or something (from a larger group).
To gather, collect.

To select (animals, plants, humans, etc) from a group and then kill (them) in a controlled manner, typically to reduce the numbers of the group or remove group members who have an undesirable characteristic.
(Should we delete this redundant sense?) To kill (an animal, person, etc), for any reason.
To lay off in order to reduce the numbers of; get rid of.
senses.example: The company culled more employees this month.

senses.definition: To selectively not render or process certain objects, such as polygons.
senses.example: back-face culling

senses.definition: A selection.
An organized killing of selected animals.
An individual animal selected to be killed, or item of produce to be discarded.
A lobster having only one claw.
A piece unfit for inclusion within a larger group; an inferior specimen.
The act of laying off employees.

core.definition: To select and remove certain animals or items from a group, often by killing them to control numbers.

pronunciation.tip: One short syllable with the same vowel as 'cut' or 'hut'. End with a clear l sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it sounds clinical and sometimes harsh, especially about animals or people.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'cull' appears mostly in farming, wildlife management and agriculture, such as 'culling a herd'. It can also mean selecting the best items from a group, like culling photos. Using it for people can sound cold, so be careful.

distinctions.note: 'Select' is neutral and positive; 'cull' suggests removing the weaker or unwanted members of a group.
'Kill' is general; 'cull' implies a planned, controlled removal of selected members of a group.

examples.everyday: I'm going to cull my closet this weekend and give away the clothes I never wear.
examples.professional: We need to cull the duplicate records from the customer database before the migration.
examples.analytical: The philosopher warns that any system that culls its members by a single measure of worth will eventually discard what it cannot measure.

nuance.analogy: Culling is like pruning a garden: you cut away what is weak or excess so the rest can grow.
nuance.etymology: From Latin colligere, to collect, through Middle English culle, to pick out.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'cull' with 'call' or 'kill' in pronunciation or meaning.
Using 'cull' for simply picking something up; it implies selection and removal.

cull.etymology: From Middle English *cullen*, *cuilen*, *coilen*, from Old French *cuillir* (“collect, gather, select”), from Latin *colligō* (“gather together”).

senses.definition: A period or condition when food is rare and hence expensive; famine.
Scarcity; a lack or short supply.

core.definition: A serious lack or shortage of something needed or wanted.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a r-colored vowel, so say durth, rhyming with birth. Do not pronounce the ea as a long e or the r as a separate sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a noticeable shortage that is a problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dearth in writing, news, academic prose, and formal speech, often as 'a dearth of evidence' or 'a dearth of qualified candidates.' It sounds stiff in casual conversation, where people usually say 'not enough' or 'a lack of.' The historical sense of famine is now archaic.

distinctions.note: Shortage is common and practical for supply problems, while dearth is more formal and often emphasizes an absence felt as a loss.
Scarcity is a more technical or economic word for limited resources, while dearth is more literary and rhetorical.

examples.everyday: There's a dearth of good parking downtown, so take the bus if you can.
examples.professional: The report notes a dearth of experienced data engineers in our region, which slows the project.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the dearth of primary sources makes any confident claim about the early church speculative.

nuance.analogy: A dearth is like a pantry with almost nothing left on its shelves.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English derthe, from dere, dear, meaning costly, from Old English dēore.
common_mistakes: Using dearth with a verb of sudden loss, as in 'the dearth happened,' instead of 'there was a dearth.'
Confusing dearth with death or dear in pronunciation.

dearth.etymology: First attested at least as early as the late 1300s, and appearing in Tyndale’s Pentateuch (1530) as well as the Coverdale Bible (1535).

senses.definition: In a decisive manner.

core.definition: In a firm way that settles a matter or ends doubt; without hesitation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SY, with a long I. The -ly ending is light and unstressed, so it should not sound like a separate beat.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing firm action or a clear win; neutral when describing a result.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use decisively in sports, politics and business to describe a clear outcome, such as winning decisively. In casual speech people more often say 'by a lot' or 'big time'. It is natural after verbs like act, win, answer or respond.

distinctions.note: Clearly means plainly or obviously, while decisively means with finality that ends doubt.
Firmly describes strength of grip or conviction, while decisively describes the way a matter is settled.

examples.everyday: Our team beat them decisively, so the rest of the season should be fun.
examples.professional: The board acted decisively and cut the budget by a third within a week.
examples.analytical: The author argues decisively that the policy failed, although the data supports only a weaker claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a final buzzer, decisively ends the game without any doubt about the score.
nuance.etymology: Formed from decisive and the adverb suffix -ly; see decisive.
common_mistakes: Placing decisively between the subject and verb in a way that sounds awkward; American English usually puts it before the verb or at the end of the clause.
Mispronouncing the stress as dih-si-SIVE-lee.

senses.definition: That declares a construct.
Of or relating to declarative programming.
Serving to declare; having the quality of a declaration.
Expressing truth.
Synonym of declaration (declarative statement)

(Ithkuil linguistics) Illocution: a “performative” statement which. by its utterance/publication, creates a change of state (at least psychologically) for the addressees (i.e. a declaration, announcement, edict, etc.)

core.definition: In software engineering, describing what result a program should produce rather than the step-by-step process to compute it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KLAIR, the second syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, so the second vowel sounds like a quick 'uh', not 'eh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers use declarative for configuration tools, databases and query languages that state the desired outcome. In grammar, declarative means a sentence that states a fact, and Americans learn that term in school. The noun sense, meaning a declarative statement, is rare in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Imperative describes listing steps to execute, while declarative describes the desired result.
Descriptive means describing something in detail, while declarative means asserting it as a statement or specification.

examples.everyday: My son's grammar worksheet asked us to turn each question into a declarative sentence.
examples.professional: We switched the deployment to a declarative configuration so the system reconciles the actual state with the desired state.
examples.analytical: Declarative descriptions of knowledge separate what is true from how it is inferred.

nuance.analogy: A declarative specification is like a recipe that lists the finished dish, leaving the cook to decide the steps.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin declarativus, from declarare 'to make clear'.
common_mistakes: Confusing declarative with declaration, which is the noun.
Stressing the wrong syllable or pronouncing the middle vowels too clearly.

senses.definition: Harmful, often in a subtle or unexpected way.
senses.example: deleterious effects

senses.definition: Having lower fitness.
senses.example: A deleterious mutation

core.definition: Harmful, often in a subtle, gradual, or unexpected way, especially to health, relationships, or systems.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on TEER, the third syllable, and the -ious ending is two syllables in General American, so it sounds like TEER-ee-us. The r is strongly pronounced, and the middle syllables are reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It is used when a harmful effect is subtle or long-term, so it sounds more precise and more serious than bad or harmful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deleterious mostly in writing, science, medicine, policy, and careful analysis, not in casual talk. In conversation, people usually say harmful, bad for you, or damaging. Using it in a meeting can sound precise and a bit formal, which is fine in a report.

distinctions.note: Harmful is common and everyday. Deleterious is more formal and often implies a subtle or cumulative harm to a system or body.
Detrimental is equally formal and often used in business writing. Deleterious leans more toward biology, health, and chemistry, where the effect is gradual.
Toxic refers to poison or a very hostile environment. Deleterious is broader and does not require a poison or obvious hostility.

examples.everyday: My doctor said too much late-night screen time can be deleterious to my sleep.
examples.professional: The outage had a deleterious impact on customer trust, so we need a clear postmortem.
examples.analytical: The author argues that unexamined certainty has deleterious effects on both moral reasoning and institutional humility.

nuance.analogy: Like rust creeping under paint: you do not notice the damage at first, but over time it weakens the whole structure.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin deleterius, from Greek deletērios (harmful), from deletēr (destroyer).
common_mistakes: Using deleterious for things that are simply bad or unpleasant, where harmful or bad would be more natural.
Saying deleterious of instead of deleterious to or deleterious for, the usual prepositions in American writing.

deleterious.etymology: Adapted borrowing (1640s; 1582 as *deletorious*) of *ous*, from Ancient Greek *δηλητήριος* (“noxious, deleterious”), from *δηλητήρ* (“a destroyer”), from *δηλέομαι* (“I hurt, damage, spoil, waste”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to demography.
A demographic criterion: a characteristic used to classify people for statistical purposes, such as age, race, or gender.
A demographic group: a collection of people sharing a value for a certain demographic criterion.
An individual person's characteristic, encoded for the purposes of statistical analysis.
senses.example: (The addition of quotations indicative of this usage is being sought:)

core.definition: Adjective: relating to the statistics of human populations. Noun: a group of people defined by shared characteristics such as age, income, or location.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on GRAF, and the first syllable is a strong dem. In the American r, the tongue curls back, and the final -ic is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical and objective term, though marketing uses can sound impersonal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use demographic often in business, marketing, politics, and news, as both an adjective and a noun. Saying target demographic is very common. In casual conversation, people sometimes say group or crowd, but demographic is widely understood and not unusual.

distinctions.note: Demography is the scientific study of populations, while demographic is the adjective or noun used for the characteristics or groups within that study.
Demographics is the plural noun for population characteristics, often used in marketing, while demographic is more often used as an adjective or for a single group.

examples.everyday: My friend works in marketing and says the new coffee shop is trying to reach a younger demographic.
examples.professional: The product team wants to see the demographic breakdown of users before we finalize the launch plan.
examples.analytical: The analysis treats each demographic variable as a potentially confounding factor in estimating the effect of income on health.

nuance.analogy: A demographic is like a sorting label on a mailing list, grouping people by traits that matter for a particular question.
nuance.etymology: From demography plus -ic, from Greek dēmos, people, and -graphia, writing or description.
common_mistakes: Using demographic as a verb.
Confusing demographic, the adjective, with demographics, the noun for population characteristics.

senses.definition: To have an unfavorable opinion of; to deprecate or disapprove of.
To abash, embarrass or disconcert.
To refuse countenance or support to; to discourage.
Cold treatment; disapprobation.

core.definition: To make someone feel embarrassed or disapproved of, or to refuse to support something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable KOWN, and reduce the later vowels to a soft uh sound. The word ends with -ance, pronounced nuns, not nance.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests disapproval or embarrassment, usually expressed quietly and politely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use discountenance in conversation. You will meet it in literature, formal essays, and older books. In everyday speech, people say embarrass, disapprove of, or not support. If you use it, it sounds deliberately formal.

distinctions.note: Embarrass is the everyday word for making someone feel awkward; discountenance is more formal and can imply a cold, disapproving stare.
Disapprove is clear and common; discountenance is formal and often stresses refusing support or showing coldness.

examples.professional: The committee will discountenance any proposal that does not include a budget.
examples.analytical: Scholars have long noted that the council chose to discountenance the reform rather than debate it openly.

nuance.analogy: To discountenance someone is like giving them a cold look across a crowded room: nothing is said, but the message is clear.
nuance.etymology: From French décontenancer, from dés- (un-) and contenance (bearing, demeanor), from Latin continentia.
common_mistakes: Using discountenance to mean discount in shopping contexts.
Spelling it discountance, which is incorrect.

senses.definition: Wasteful of health or possessions in the pursuit of pleasure.
senses.example: He recalled his dissipated youth spent in nightclubs and bars.

core.definition: Living a wild, self-indulgent life that wastes health, money, or time on pleasure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ed is a short id sound, and it is not a separate syllable like ayt-ed.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies moral decline, excess, or a tired, worn-out look.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dissipated in literary descriptions, older novels, and formal critique of someone's lifestyle. In everyday speech they would say wild, run-down, or partying too much. The word can also describe a worn appearance, such as a dissipated face, so it works for both behavior and looks.

distinctions.note: Dissolute is more formal and focuses on immoral looseness, while dissipated emphasizes wasted health and money through overindulgence.
Wild is casual and can be positive, while dissipated is always negative and suggests exhaustion or moral waste.

examples.everyday: After a few years of partying every weekend, he started to look pretty dissipated.
examples.professional: Calling a candidate dissipated in a hiring review would be unprofessional, so stick to facts about performance.
examples.analytical: The novel's dissipated aristocrat stands for a culture that has lost its moral purpose.

nuance.analogy: A dissipated person is like a phone battery drained by too many apps: the resource is spent before its real work is done.
nuance.etymology: From the past participle of dissipate, from Latin dissipare 'to scatter'.
common_mistakes: Using dissipated only to mean scattered or dispersed; in American English it usually describes a wasteful, excessive lifestyle.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable as dih-SIP-ay-tid.

senses.definition: The quality of being docile.
senses.example: Couldn't docility from totalitarian indoctrination be a human shortcoming?

core.definition: The quality of being easy to manage, teach, or direct, and willing to accept instruction without resistance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SIL, the second syllable. The final syllable -ty is a light tee, and the middle vowel is reduced to uh. Do not stress the first syllable or stretch the -ty ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context; it can be praise for a willing learner or criticism of someone who never questions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use docility mostly in written or formal discussion, such as a book on education or psychology. In everyday speech they would more often say easygoing or cooperative. Describing a person's docility can be a veiled insult, so be careful when using it about a colleague or friend.

distinctions.note: Obedience is the act of following commands, while docility is a general disposition to be led and taught.
Meekness is a gentle, humble character quality, while docility is specifically a readiness to accept direction and instruction.

examples.everyday: Her docility at the vet surprised everyone, since she usually fights the exam table.
examples.professional: Management mistook the team's docility during the reorganization for agreement, when people were simply afraid to object.
examples.analytical: For Foucault, docility is produced by disciplinary power rather than being a natural trait of the body.

nuance.analogy: Docility is like a well-trained dog that comes when called, not because it has no will, but because it has learned to trust its trainer.
nuance.etymology: From Latin docilitas, teachableness, from docilis, teachable.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying dah-sih-LIT-ee instead of dah-SIL-uh-tee.
Confusing docility with docile as a verb; docility is only a noun.

senses.definition: To set a boundary, rule, or limit, especially on what one will tolerate.
senses.example: I don't mind if they have some fun, but I draw the line at anything that might harm others.

core.definition: To set a limit on what you will accept, tolerate, or do, and refuse to go past it.

pronunciation.tip: The word 'the' reduces to 'thuh' before a consonant, and in fast speech 'draw the line' links smoothly into 'draw-thuh-LINE.' Stress the word line, not draw.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes a firm boundary, and it can be used with humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I draw the line at...' when they refuse something, such as 'I draw the line at cleaning other people's dishes.' A natural reply is 'Fair enough' or 'I get it.' It can sound stubborn if used rudely, so soften it with a friendly tone.

distinctions.note: Set limits is more formal and neutral; draw the line suggests a firm refusal at a specific point.
Stand firm describes holding a position under pressure; draw the line describes stating exactly where the boundary is.

collocations: know where to draw the line

examples.everyday: I'll help you move, but I draw the line at carrying the piano.
examples.professional: We have to draw the line on scope creep, or the project will never ship.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long asked where to draw the line between persuasion and manipulation in public debate.

nuance.analogy: Like a painter drawing a border on a map, you mark exactly where your acceptance stops.
nuance.etymology: Draw from Old English dragan; line from Latin linea, a linen thread.
common_mistakes: Saying 'draw a line' when you mean 'draw the line'; the article matters because it refers to a specific limit.
Using 'draw the line to' instead of 'draw the line at' or 'draw the line on.'

conversation.text: I'll help with the report, but I draw the line at working on Sunday.
Kids can have some screen time, but we draw the line at phones at dinner.
We need to draw the line somewhere on scope, or this project will never end.

senses.definition: To put on special or fancy clothes.
senses.example: Everyone dressed up for the graduation ball.

senses.definition: To put on a costume portraying oneself as a particular type of character or well-known person.
senses.example: We're having a party on Saturday, but you must dress up as a famous historical figure.

senses.definition: To put a costume on (someone) portraying them as a particular type of character or well-known person.
senses.example: The cat hated when they dressed him up for Halloween.

senses.definition: To decorate; to prettify.
To present in a favorable light.
senses.example: You can dress up that proposal however you want; it's still going to go over like a lead balloon.

core.definition: To put on formal or fancy clothes, or to wear a costume to look like someone else.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on 'up', the particle, in this phrase. In fast speech 'dress up' links into one flowing sound, with 'up' stressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it can mean making an effort for a special occasion, or playing a character for fun.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'dress up' to mean wearing nicer clothes for an event, as in 'Should we dress up for dinner?' For costumes, people say 'dress up as' something, like 'dress up as a pirate' for Halloween. A natural reply is 'Sure, I'll dress up' or 'No need, casual is fine.'

distinctions.note: 'Get dressed' means putting on clothes at all; 'dress up' means putting on nicer clothes than usual.
'Dress down' means wearing casual clothes, often for a workplace on a relaxed day.

examples.everyday: Do we need to dress up for Aunt Linda's birthday dinner?
examples.professional: The team agreed to dress up for the client presentation on Thursday.
examples.analytical: Scholars note that the medieval pilgrims dressed up in penitential garb to signal their devotion.

nuance.analogy: Like putting a clean shirt and a tie on a plain outfit to look ready for a special event.
nuance.etymology: 'Dress' comes from Old French 'dresser', to arrange or prepare; 'up' is the adverb of completion or display.
common_mistakes: Separating the phrase incorrectly; say 'dress up for dinner', not 'dress for up dinner'.
Using 'dress up' for simply getting dressed in the morning.

conversation.text: You don't have to dress up, it's a casual barbecue.
My son is dressing up as Spider-Man for Halloween.
A little salsa really dresses up plain eggs.

senses.definition: A style of dynamic typing in which an object's current set of methods and properties determines the valid semantics, rather than its inheritance from a particular class or implementation of a specific interface.

core.definition: A programming style where an object is judged usable by the methods and properties it has, not by its declared class or interface.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun, the first word 'duck' usually gets the main stress, and 'typing' gets a weaker stress. Keep 'typing' short and light, with the 'i' sound as in 'eye' in the stressed first syllable of 'TY-ping'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a positive design term in software communities, often praised for flexibility, though it can make errors appear only at runtime.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers in the US use 'duck typing' in code reviews, design discussions, and documentation, especially for Python, Ruby, and JavaScript. It comes from the saying 'If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck.' Outside programming, the phrase is not used.

distinctions.note: Static typing checks types at compile time against declared types, while duck typing checks behavior at runtime.
Interfaces are explicit contracts that code declares; duck typing relies on the object actually supporting the methods it is called with.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the Python code uses duck typing, so it doesn't matter what class the object is as long as it has the right methods.
examples.professional: Let's use duck typing in the pipeline so it accepts any object that implements fit and predict, not just our base class.
examples.analytical: Duck typing moves the locus of type safety from declared hierarchies to observable behavior, which increases flexibility at the cost of earlier error detection.

nuance.analogy: It is like a bouncer who lets anyone in who can show a valid pass, rather than checking the guest list by name.
nuance.etymology: From the duck test, a humorous saying popularized in the early 20th century, applied to programming in the 2000s.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'typing' as the main word, as in 'duck TY-ping', when the compound stress usually falls on 'DUCK'.
Thinking duck typing means the code checks the animal species; it checks only whether the required methods exist.

duck-typing.etymology: From the so-called duck test: “if it looks like a duck, swims like a duck, and quacks like a duck, then it probably is a duck.”

senses.definition: A person who has been deceived.
A duplicate. Often:
A duplicate of a photographic image.
A duplicate of an order receipt printed for kitchen staff.
A word which appears more than once in a crossword puzzle.
A counterfeit; a fake, a (typically cheaper) copy (of some legitimate consumer product, design, etc).
An unanticipated method or incident by which duplicates of in-game items are created; a duplication glitch.
An in-game item that was created by means of a duplication glitch.
To swindle, deceive, or trick.
To duplicate.
senses.example: Can you dupe this photo for me?

core.definition: To trick or deceive someone, especially into giving money, or believing something false.

pronunciation.tip: It rhymes with loop and hoop. Keep the vowel long and the p crisp; do not add a y sound or a second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone was fooled, often in a way that makes them look naive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dupe in news, crime stories, and everyday talk about being tricked, like being duped by a scam email. As a noun, a dupe is a person who has been fooled. It is slightly informal, so in formal writing people may choose deceive or mislead. A natural reply to being tricked might be Oh no, how did that happen?

distinctions.note: Deceive is the general, formal word for causing someone to believe something false; dupe is more informal and often implies the victim was easily fooled.
A scam is the scheme itself or a dishonest plan, while dupe describes the act of tricking a particular person.

examples.everyday: I got duped by a fake online sale, so now I check the seller before I pay.
examples.professional: Our fraud team found that the vendor had duped several clients into signing contracts they did not understand.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that propaganda works best when it does not feel like deception, leaving the audience to believe they are not being duped.

nuance.analogy: Being duped is like following a map that someone has deliberately drawn wrong: you trust it, and it leads you away from the truth.
nuance.etymology: Originally a 1800s American slang term, possibly from dupe, a decoy bird, or from the word duping, meaning to dupe.
common_mistakes: Using dupe as a noun for a copy; in modern English it usually means a person who has been fooled.
Saying dupe someone of something when the natural pattern is dupe someone into doing something.

dupe.etymology: From French *duper*, from Middle French *duppe*, alteration of *huppe* (“hoopoe”), from Latin.

senses.definition: Relating to ecology, the interrelationships of organisms and their environment.
Not harmful to the environment.

core.definition: Relating to ecology, the relationships among living things and their environment; in everyday use, also meaning environmentally friendly.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LAH, the third syllable, with a light secondary stress on the first. The final syllable is a weak 'kul', not a separate 'ih' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: In science, ecological describes the relationships of organisms to each other and their habitats, while in everyday American speech it often means environmentally friendly or sustainable, as in ecological cleaning products. Americans commonly say 'eco-friendly' as a synonym. The technical sense is common in biology and environmental policy.

distinctions.note: Environmental covers anything about the surroundings, including pollution and policy, while ecological focuses on how living things relate to one another and their habitats.
Eco-friendly is an informal everyday phrase for products or practices that harm nature less, while ecological is more formal and scientific.

examples.everyday: I switched to ecological cleaning products because they're gentler on the rivers near our house.
examples.professional: The sustainability team wants our packaging to have a lower ecological footprint, so we're reviewing materials.
examples.analytical: Her argument depends on an ecological model in which species relationships shape the stability of the whole system.

nuance.analogy: Like a neighborhood in which every household depends on the others for water, food and shelter.
nuance.etymology: From ecology, coined from Greek oikos, 'house', and -logia, 'study of'.
common_mistakes: Using ecological as a synonym for eco-friendly in technical writing, where it means relating to ecology, not merely green.
Pronouncing the word with the stress on the first syllable instead of LAH.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the universal Church, representing the entire Christian world; interdenominational; sometimes by extension, interreligious.
(rare) General; universal; catholic; worldwide.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Relating to the whole Christian church, or to cooperation among different Christian denominations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on MEN. The first part sounds like "ek-yuh", and the "-ical" ending reduces to "ih-kul". Don't say "eh-KYOO-muh-nik".

nuance.connotation: Positive in church and academic settings. It suggests unity and openness, though some conservative believers may distrust it when it implies doctrinal compromise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ecumenical in church news, seminaries, and interfaith or Christian unity events, such as "an ecumenical service." It is rarely used in casual conversation. In the US it is often paired with "interfaith" but the two words are not the same: ecumenical is about Christian churches, while interfaith includes other religions.

distinctions.note: Ecumenical refers mainly to Christian churches working together; interfaith refers to cooperation among different religions.
Universal means worldwide or applying to everyone; ecumenical specifically refers to the unity of the Christian church.

examples.everyday: Our church hosts an ecumenical Thanksgiving service with Methodists and Lutherans.
examples.professional: Our nonprofit runs an ecumenical outreach program that works across denominations.
examples.analytical: Ecumenical dialogue requires honesty about doctrinal differences as well as shared commitments.

nuance.analogy: An ecumenical gathering is like a potluck where every congregation brings its own dish to the same table.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin oecumenicus, from Greek oikoumenikos, "of the inhabited world", from oikoumene.
common_mistakes: Using "ecumenical" to mean "economical" or "economic" by mistake.
Using "ecumenical" as a noun for a person; the noun is "ecumenist".
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word oikoumene, meaning "the inhabited world", appears in Luke 2:1, where a decree goes out for all the world to be enrolled. Later it came to mean the whole Christian church. Key passages include John 17:21, where Jesus prays that his followers may all be one, and Ephesians 4:3-6, which speaks of one body and one Spirit.

senses.definition: Marked by or resulting from extraordinary ability to recall detailed and vivid mental images of visual images.
senses.example: an eidetic memory

senses.definition: Of or relating to the essential forms of a phenomena.

core.definition: Having an unusually vivid visual memory, able to recall an image or scene in fine detail as if still seeing it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, DET. Say the first syllable as the word 'eye', not 'ee'; the final -tic is short, like 'ik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it praises a remarkable memory, but it is a specialized word that can sound pretentious in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eidetic mostly in psychology, education, and writing about memory. In everyday speech they would say 'she has a photographic memory' or 'she remembers everything she sees.' The philosophical sense, relating to essential forms, is rare in American English.

distinctions.note: Eidetic memory is the scientific term for vivid visual recall; 'photographic memory' is the popular term, and experts doubt that it exists in a literal sense.
Exceptional is a general word for unusually good; eidetic names one specific kind of memory.

examples.everyday: My son can look at a page for a few seconds and recite it back, which is almost eidetic.
examples.professional: The study tested whether participants with eidetic memory retained the layout of the slides better than others.
examples.analytical: Husserl's appeal to eidetic intuition assumes that essences can be grasped through imaginative variation, not only through sensory memory.

nuance.analogy: An eidetic memory is like a camera that never loses its photos.
nuance.etymology: From Greek eidetikos, 'relating to seeing or form', from eidos, 'form, shape'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'ee-DET-ik' with the wrong first vowel.
Using it to mean simply 'good at remembering' rather than vivid visual recall.

eidetic.etymology: From German *eidetisch*, from Ancient Greek *εἰδητικός*, from *εἶδος* (“form”).

core.definition: Having eight strings; in the Bible, a term linked to the Hebrew word sheminith, a musical instrument or tuning in the Psalms and Chronicles.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, EIGHT, and the second word, STRINGED, is also stressed. Keep the 'ng' in strings and do not add a vowel before the final d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a descriptive term with religious and archaic associations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use eight-stringed except when describing instruments, usually in Bible study, music history, or academic writing. In everyday speech they would say 'an eight-string guitar' or 'an eight-string instrument.' The term is mostly found in older translations and commentaries.

distinctions.note: Ten-stringed appears in Psalms 33 and 144 for a different instrument; eight-stringed relates to the Hebrew sheminith.
A lyre is the kind of instrument; eight-stringed describes how many strings it has.

examples.everyday: My daughter's guitar is an eight-stringed one, which surprised me when we bought it.
examples.professional: The music teacher explained that the eight-stringed instrument mentioned in the psalm was tuned an octave lower.
examples.analytical: Commentators debate whether the phrase 'according to the sheminith' refers to an eight-stringed instrument or to a musical octave.

nuance.analogy: An eight-stringed instrument is like a guitar with four extra strings, giving a wider range of notes.
nuance.etymology: Compound of eight, from Old English eahta, and stringed, from Old English streng, 'cord'.
common_mistakes: Confusing eight-stringed with eight-string, which is an informal guitar name.
Assuming it is a standard English term for an instrument; it is mainly used in Bible translations and commentary.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase in English translations usually renders the Hebrew word sheminith (שְׁמִינִית), meaning 'eighth' or 'octave', which likely refers to a musical tuning or an instrument with eight strings. It appears in the superscriptions of Psalm 6 and Psalm 12, and in 1 Chronicles 15:21. The passages say little about the instrument itself, so scholars differ on its exact nature.

senses.definition: Capable of stretching; particularly, capable of stretching so as to return to an original shape or size when force is released.
senses.example: The rope is somewhat elastic, so expect it to give when you pull on it.

senses.definition: Made of elastic.
senses.example: elastic band

senses.definition: Of clothing, elasticated.
Sensitive to changes in price.
senses.example: Demand for entertainment is more elastic than demand for energy.

senses.definition: Springy; bouncy; vivacious.
Pervasive, all-encompassing.
Able to return quickly to a former state or condition, after being depressed or overtaxed; having power to recover easily from shocks and trials.
senses.example: elastic spirits; an elastic constitution

senses.definition: An elastic material used in clothing, particularly in waistbands and cuffs.
senses.example: running shorts use elastic to eliminate the need for a belt

senses.definition: An elastic band.
Specifically, a hair tie.

core.definition: Able to stretch and then return to its original shape or size when the stretching force is removed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, 'LAS'. The final -ic is a short 'ik', not 'eek'. The a is a short American 'a' as in 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes flexibility and resilience, and can be used metaphorically for flexible schedules or rules.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'elastic' for stretchy materials, such as waistbands, cuffs, and fabric. As a noun, 'elastic' means the stretchy material itself. In everyday American English, 'rubber band' is the common word for the loop of stretchy rubber, while 'elastic band' sounds more British. Metaphorical uses, like 'an elastic deadline', are common in business.

distinctions.note: Flexible means able to bend or adapt, without necessarily returning to shape. Elastic specifically means it springs back to its original form.
Stretchy is an informal everyday word for fabric or material that stretches. Elastic is more precise and technical.

examples.everyday: These pants have an elastic waistband, so they're comfortable for a long day of walking.
examples.professional: We chose an elastic cloud architecture so the service can handle sudden traffic spikes without manual intervention.
examples.analytical: The concept of an elastic constitution suggests a framework that can absorb new circumstances while preserving its original principles.

nuance.analogy: Like a rubber band that snaps back into shape after you let it go.
nuance.etymology: From Modern Latin elasticus, from Greek elaunein ('to drive, propel').
common_mistakes: Calling a rubber band an 'elastic band' in everyday American speech, which sounds British.
Confusing the adjective 'elastic' with the noun 'elastics', which in American English usually means rubber bands or hair ties.

elastic.etymology: From French *élastique*, from New Latin *elasticus* (“elastic”), from Ancient Greek *ἐλαστός*, alternative form of *ἐλατός* (“ductile”) (cf.

senses.definition: To raise (something) to a higher position.
senses.example: The doctor told me elevating my legs would help reduce the swelling.

senses.definition: To promote (someone) to a higher rank.
senses.example: Did you forget that all programs that modify the registry need to be elevated?

senses.definition: To temporarily grant a program additional security privileges to the system to perform a privileged action (usually on the program's request).
senses.example: Did you forget that all programs that modify the registry need to be elevated?

senses.definition: To confer honor or nobility on (someone).
senses.example: The traditional worldview elevates man as the pinnacle of creation.

senses.definition: To make (something or someone) more worthy or of greater value.
senses.example: A talented chef can elevate everyday ingredients into gourmet delights.

senses.definition: To direct (the mind, thoughts, etc.) toward more worthy things.
To increase the intensity or degree of (something).
senses.example: Some drugs have the side effect of elevating your blood sugar level.

senses.definition: (dated) To increase the loudness of (a sound, especially one's voice).
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To intoxicate in a slight degree; to make (someone) tipsy.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To raise something to a higher position or level, or to promote someone to a higher rank or status.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EL. The middle syllable is a quick reduced uh, not 'ee'. Don't add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests improvement, honor or uplift.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use elevate in business, politics and formal writing when someone moves up in rank or quality improves. In casual talk people more often say raise, move up or bump up. Elevate is also a common term in computing, where it means granting a program extra permissions.

distinctions.note: Raise is the everyday, neutral word for lifting or increasing something. Elevate sounds more formal and suggests moving someone or something to a higher status or standard.
Promote is the standard word for advancing someone at work. Elevate is more formal or figurative and can describe ideas, tastes or conversation as well.

collocations: elevate someone to a leadership role

examples.everyday: Adding fresh herbs really elevates a simple pasta dish.
examples.professional: The board decided to elevate Maria to senior director after her team doubled the revenue.
examples.analytical: Aristotle argues that tragedy elevates the audience by purging pity and fear through the representation of human suffering.

nuance.analogy: Like a hydraulic lift that raises a car to a higher level so people can work on it more easily.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elevatus, the past participle of elevare, meaning to lift up.
common_mistakes: Using elevate for a physical object in casual speech, where raise or lift is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
